help.business-exports.note4: Where the box goes to the port by rail — or came inland by rail on an import — keep the railway’s note under “The railway’s note”: its copy or its number, and tick what is printed on it. You are asked only what the rules of its route ask for: the CIM between its member states, the SMGS between Russia, China and Central Asia, or the railway’s own conditions, such as Kenya Railways’. You are told what is missing, what a gap costs if something goes wrong, and whether its box number and seals agree with ours. The railway issues the note; SeeBuyGet keeps it, and issues none.
help.business-parcels.title: Sending parcels from your business
help.business-parcels.summary: Parcels go from a shop or your own place to a shop or your own place, and are paid from your parcel balance, the way a store pays: no balance, no label. The person collecting it shows the code you pass on.
help.business-parcels.step1: Under Parcels, open a parcel account once. It is a balance with the SeeBuyGet company in your country.
help.business-parcels.step2: “Top up”: give the amount and the phone that pays, and approve the prompt on it — or pay by paybill with the reference shown. The balance grows once the payment is confirmed, never before.
help.business-parcels.step3: “Send a parcel”: the shop it is handed in at, the shop it is collected at, the phone of who collects it, its four measurements and a photo of what is inside. The price is shown before you send; it is paid from the balance at once, and its label prints.
help.business-parcels.step4: Open a parcel to print its label — it opens in a slide-up on its page, with Print under it — see where it is, and copy the code the shop asks for. Pass the code to whoever collects it: SeeBuyGet sends them no text.
help.business-parcels.note1: Why a balance: a parcel is paid when it is sent, so a shop never takes in a parcel nobody has paid for, and nobody waits for an invoice. What is held for the longest route and not spent comes back once it is collected.
help.business-parcels.note2: Not enough in the balance: the parcel is made without a label, and “Pay now” pays it after you top up. Called off before it is handed in, its money comes back in full; at a hub it comes back to the shop it was handed in at, for the price shown.
help.business-parcels.note3: A load of your own, or something too big for a shop — a pallet, a machine — goes under Domestic, where you agree its price with the carrier. Parcels across a border are not sent from here yet.
help.business-parcels.note4: Your own system can send them too. With a company key, made by an owner under Business details, it sends a parcel through the same checks and pays from the same balance; a test key prices it and keeps nothing. Where your system’s address is given, it is told each step: paid, handed in, ready to collect, collected, called off.
help.business-parcels.note5: Collected from your place instead of a shop: under “Collected from your place”, choose one of your places where goods are loaded. It takes the delivery area of the shop nearest it, and must have one within 30 km. Parcels sent from there wait for you to bag them by where they go; close each bag with its seal’s number and a photo, and the drivers near are told it is ready.
help.business-parcels.note6: Delivered to your place instead of collected at a shop: choose one of your places under “Collected at”, and the most you will pay a driver for the last leg. The parcel goes to the shop nearest that place; once it is there, a driver is asked to bring it, at their own price and never above your most, paid from your balance when they take it. The shop hands it only to that driver, by their pass, and whoever signs at your place is on its record. If your balance does not hold the most by then, nothing is posted and you are told; and it can always be collected at the shop with its code. While a driver is being found, its free days on the shelf do not run out and the person receiving it is not told to come for it; if no driver takes it in a day, you are told, so you can raise the most. If its free days ran out while your balance was short, what the shop is owed for keeping it is paid from your balance when it is handed over.
help.business-fbl.title: A forwarder’s bill of lading
help.business-fbl.summary: The bill of lading a freight forwarder issues on FIATA’s form — an FBL, or its waybill, the FWB — can be kept on an export or an import, with what is printed on it. SeeBuyGet issues none and vouches for none: it says whether the bill is complete as printed, whether it agrees with our own papers, where you can check it is genuine, and what it means if something goes wrong.
help.business-fbl.step1: Under the export or the import, “The forwarder’s bill of lading › Keep the bill”. Choose the bill of lading or the waybill, and give its number, the forwarder that issued it and the day. A paper bill is kept as a copy from your papers; an electronic one by its number. Tick each box of the form that is filled in, and write the box number, seals, packages, weight and ports as printed.
help.business-fbl.step2: Read it back: what the form asks for and is missing, and whether the box, seals, packages, weight and port agree with ours. Agreeing proves nothing about whether it is genuine — a forged bill can copy every number.
help.business-fbl.step3: An electronic bill: open FIATA’s verification page from the bill, upload it or type its number, and keep what the page showed among your papers. Then record it on the bill — registered or not, and the number and issuer the page showed — with the result attached. It is your record of what you saw, shown with your name: SeeBuyGet checks nothing. A paper bill has no public check: its serial number is with the association whose emblem it carries.
help.business-fbl.step4: Is a forwarder or a clearing agent a FIATA member? Look it up yourself in FIATA’s directory, under its country — the link is beside the bill and where you choose a clearing agent. SeeBuyGet checks nobody’s membership.
help.business-fbl.note1: Why SeeBuyGet never issues one: whoever issues a FIATA bill of lading answers as the carrier for the whole journey, the sea included, and must be insured for it. We carry the road and keep the papers.
help.business-fbl.note2: The bill of lading is title to the goods. They are handed over against one original, surrendered duly endorsed; the copy you keep here is never an original. In Kenya and Uganda the law on electronic documents does not reach documents of title, so an electronic bill may not count as one there.
help.business-fbl.note3: The limits are said in SDR, as the bill states them, with an approximate dollar figure at a rate we keep with its date: at most 666.67 SDR a package or 2 SDR a kilogram where there is a sea leg, 8.33 SDR a kilogram where there is none. Report damage you could not see within 6 days of delivery; bring a claim to court within 9 months.
help.air-export.title: Send goods out by air
help.air-export.summary: Record the booking the airline or your forwarder confirmed, and SeeBuyGet carries the road to the airline’s cargo terminal before its latest acceptance time — chilled goods kept in their own range, secured cargo sealed. The air waybill is checked, never issued: its number, the law of its route, and whether it agrees with your packing list. SeeBuyGet books no flight.
help.air-export.step1: “Exports › Record an export by air”. Copy the booking off the airline’s confirmation: the air waybill number (eleven digits — its last digit is checked as you type), whose waybill it is, the flights with their dates and airports, the latest acceptance time (in UTC), the pieces and weight as booked, and who receives it at the airport. Say whether the airline has confirmed it. Choose where it is loaded and the cargo terminal from your places.
help.air-export.step2: Perishable goods give the temperature range they are kept in: the truck is a reefer or an insulated body, its set-point inside the range, and every reading on the way is judged against your range, not a general one. If the plant-health inspection is at the airport, tick it: three hours are added before the latest acceptance time.
help.air-export.step3: Under the export, one line says by when the load must leave to be at the cargo terminal in time, with its working: the drive, an hour at the terminal before the latest acceptance time, and the inspection’s hours where it is at the airport. “Post the load to the cargo terminal” when the cargo is packed: a driver sees the latest acceptance time and the air waybill.
help.air-export.step4: “The air waybill” shows it read against the law of its route on its day — the convention both countries share, its limit per kilogram and the time to complain — what that law asks the waybill to show and it lacks, and where its pieces or weight disagree with your packing list. Your letter of instruction by air names the consignee and the airport of destination. “Open the handover file” for your forwarder at the terminal.
help.air-export.note1: Why the latest acceptance time and not the flight: the airline accepts cargo at its terminal up to that time, and cargo that arrives after it waits for another flight, whatever time the aircraft leaves.
help.air-export.note2: Why a booking not yet confirmed still goes: cargo is often booked on request and confirmed late. The truck may go, but the cargo may not fly on that flight — that is said on the export, the driver’s job and the handover file, and the risk of being left behind is yours.
help.air-export.note3: Secured cargo — secured by a regulated agent or known consignor before it leaves — travels in a closed vehicle that locks, never on a bike, a motorcycle or a tuk-tuk; sealed where it is loaded, its seal checked at the terminal, with a driver whose ID has been seen. Its security status is the regulated agent’s to give: SeeBuyGet gives none, and signs no declaration for it.
help.air-export.note4: Medicines and vaccines are not carried to an airport on SeeBuyGet yet. The air waybill, the flight and the acceptance are the airline’s and your forwarder’s: delivered at the terminal is not accepted by the airline.
help.air-export.note5: Live animals: choose “Live animals” as the goods and declare them — what they are, how many, the consignee’s import permit and the veterinary health certificate by number, CITES where the species is listed, who looks after them on the way, who signed the shipper’s certification, and your word that none is unfit to travel. They go on a livestock body, or crated in a closed vehicle with air; the driver looks them over and has the original papers before taking them. Day-old chicks are warned if they would pass their 72 hours — the breeder’s figure — before the flight.
help.air-export.note6: When the booking changes, say so under “The air waybill”. Confirmed after all: “The airline confirmed it”. Moved: “Another flight or time”, give the flight it is booked on now and its latest acceptance time from the new confirmation, then “Record the new booking”. The booking as it stood is kept on the export. The clock follows the new time and its warnings are said again; the load to the cargo terminal carries the new booking, and a driver already on the way is told what changed.
help.air-export.note7: At the cargo terminal the driver asks the handler for its receipt and gives its number when delivering: it is what shows the goods were in before the latest acceptance time. Anything the handler found not as booked — pieces short, a carton damaged — is said under “The air waybill” at once: tell your forwarder or the airline, because what was not accepted may not fly.
help.air-export.note8: Where the shed gives trucks a slot, record it with the booking or later under “The air waybill”. The truck is then timed to arrive by the slot’s end instead of the latest acceptance time, and its driver is told the slot and its reference. A slot that ends after the latest acceptance time is refused: the cargo could not make the flight in it.
help.air-export.note9: Built up on airline pallets or containers at your forwarder’s shed? Say how many. Only a truck with a roller floor is offered the load: it rolls them on and off whole, at the shed and at the terminal’s dock. Fleets say they have one under their vehicle’s equipment.
help.air-export.note10: Flying out of an airport in another country — a Rwandan grower’s roses from Nairobi? The country is read off the airport (or say it). The road leg then crosses the border under bond: exported at home, in transit to the cargo terminal, by a carrier that holds a transit licence there — and four hours for the border are planned into the leave-by time, our figure.
help.air-export.note11: The volume on the booking goes to the road leg: a truck whose fleet recorded a smaller load space is not offered it. A fleet records a vehicle’s load space, measured inside the body, under “Load space (m³)” on the vehicle.
help.air-import.title: Collect goods that came by air
help.air-import.summary: Air cargo waits in the handler’s shed at the airport until customs, every agency the goods need and the handler’s delivery order have released it. Record each step as it comes, and SeeBuyGet sends no truck to the shed before then — and counts the handler’s free storage, so the cargo is collected before it ends.
help.air-import.step1: “Imports › Record an import”, and choose Air under “How it comes”. Then, under “By air”, copy the air waybill (its last digit is checked as you type), the flight, whose shed it waits in, the pieces and weight, and — for goods kept cold — their range. Tick the agencies besides customs that must release these goods: the list is the destination country’s, suggested by the goods, chosen by you or your clearing agent.
help.air-import.step2: Give the handler’s free storage in hours, as on its notice or tariff, and where that figure comes from. When the handler’s notice of arrival comes, record it: the hours start then. You are told under the bell in its last six hours, and once if it ends with the cargo still there.
help.air-import.step3: Post the road leg from the shed with “Mint the road leg”, as usual. It is offered to no driver yet: the board shows them what it still waits for. Record each release as it comes — customs’ release with its number, each agency’s, the handler’s delivery order or gate pass with its number. The last one opens the road leg at once.
help.air-import.step4: If your agent says it will be out within the hour, or the shed confirmed it by phone, the importer may send the truck anyway: say why, and that a truck sent early may wait at the shed, at your cost. The releases still missing stay listed.
help.air-import.note1: Why the notice of arrival opens nothing: it says the cargo has landed, not that it may leave. A truck sent on the notice queues at the shed until customs and the agencies have released the goods, and somebody pays for the waiting.
help.air-import.note2: Why the free hours are yours to give: each handler sets its own, from its own event, in hours or days — and the one published tariff we found at Jomo Kenyatta airport dates from 2013. SeeBuyGet counts the hours you give it, and never says what an hour over costs: that is the handler’s to bill.
help.air-import.note3: Medicines and vaccines are not carried from an airport on SeeBuyGet yet: who must hold a licence to carry them is with our lawyer.
help.air-import.note4: Each step is your word or your agent’s, kept with its reference and who gave it. SeeBuyGet judges none of them and cannot say when a release will come: the service charters’ times are targets, not promises.
help.air-import.note5: Live animals: tick “Live animals” under “By air” and declare them, with your word that none is unfit to travel. The veterinary authority’s release is always asked — animals do not leave the airport without it — and the importer names the place the veterinary officer named. The road leg goes there and nowhere else, is never sent elsewhere, and does not change once posted. Only a livestock body takes livestock, only a closed vehicle with air takes crates, and the driver looks them over and has the original papers before taking them.
help.air-import.note6: Why a weekend landing is warned: in Kenya customs verification, the veterinary services, the Pharmacy and Poisons Board and the standards bureau work Monday to Friday at the airport. Cargo landing on a Saturday, a Sunday, a Friday afternoon or a day your country’s calendar marks closed may wait for the next working day — unless your agent asks for officers out of hours on Form C.1, at least 24 hours before. You are told three days ahead, while there is time to ask.
help.air-import.note7: The shed releases nothing until its own storage and handling are paid: record “The handler’s charges paid” like the other steps. The delivery order’s number and the handler’s receipt are passed to the driver, who is asked for them at the counter.
help.air-import.note8: At the shed the driver counts the pieces against the air waybill before leaving. A count that differs, or damage the driver sees, goes on the consignment note — and you are told the day by which the airline must have your written complaint: 14 days from receipt for damage under the Montreal Convention. Once the goods leave the shed on a clean receipt, damage found later looks like the road’s.
help.air-import.note9: Where the shed gives trucks a slot to collect, record it under “The truck’s slot at the shed”: the driver is told to come inside it. A truck outside its slot waits, or is turned away.
help.air-import.note10: Landed in another country than yours — a Ugandan import that lands at Nairobi? The country is read off the airport (or say it). Customs at the airport then release it for transit, the handler’s delivery order and charges as usual, and the road leg runs under bond across the border to be cleared at home: your own agencies look at it there, not in the shed.
help.air-import.note11: Collected built up on airline pallets or containers? Say how many under “By air”. Only a truck with a roller floor is offered the road leg — chilled where the goods are — and its driver is told to roll them on and off whole.
help.road-meets-rail.title: Where road meets rail
help.road-meets-rail.summary: Where a container goes part of its way by train, the truck at each end is timed to the train: to the rail terminal before the train’s cut-off, and from it only once the railway has said the box is there. SeeBuyGet runs no trains and books none. It keeps the road and the rail in step, so no truck is late for a train and none is sent to wait for one.
help.road-meets-rail.step1: An export by rail: under the export, “By rail to the port › It goes by rail”. Choose the rail terminal from your places, and give the train’s cut-off there (in UTC) and the train or rail booking reference. The cut-off must fall before the port gate closes, or the box reaches the port too late for the vessel — that is refused. Do it before you post the load to the terminal: the load then goes to the rail terminal, its driver sees the train’s cut-off, and you are told under the bell six hours before the truck must leave.
help.road-meets-rail.step2: Once the railway has brought the box inside the port gate, write when, under the same heading. From then the line’s clock counts the box inside the terminal; until then it counts it outside, because it is.
help.road-meets-rail.step3: An import by rail: under the import, “Inland by rail”. Choose the rail terminal the train brings it to, when the railway expects it, and the free days the terminal gives. The road leg from there is posted as usual and collected at the rail terminal — and no driver can take it until the railway has said the box is there. When the train leaves the port with the box, write when under “When the train left the port with it (UTC)” and “Record it”: the line’s clock outside the terminal runs from then, not from when our truck collects the box inland.
help.road-meets-rail.step4: When the railway’s arrival notice comes, the importer or its clearing agent records it there, with the notice’s number. The road leg opens at once, and the terminal’s free days start: you are told under the bell on the last free day, and once if they end with the box still there. They stop when our truck takes the box out.
help.road-meets-rail.step5: If the box is there before the notice — the terminal confirmed it by phone, the notice is late — the importer may send the truck anyway, saying why. That is the importer’s decision alone, because it pays for a truck that waits. Its reason is kept and shown beside the road leg.
help.road-meets-rail.note1: Why the truck waits for the notice: a truck sent for a box still on the train queues at the gate, its driver loses the hours and the next load, and somebody pays for the waiting. Where trains run late — on many lines in Africa, and in South Africa above all just now — the railway’s own word that the box is there is the only fact to send a truck on.
help.road-meets-rail.note2: Why the train’s cut-off comes before the gate’s: a box handed to the railway after its train’s cut-off waits for the next train, and a train that reaches the port after the gate closes misses the vessel. Both are caught here, before a truck is sent, rather than at the quay.
help.road-meets-rail.note3: A driver sees a load waiting for its train on the board, with the reason, and cannot take it yet; it opens by itself once the arrival is recorded. A load taken before the rail leg was recorded is never taken back from its driver: the import says so, so that they can be told.
help.road-meets-rail.note4: The railway’s own note — its consignment note or waybill — is kept beside it, under “The railway’s note”, and checked against the rules of its route.
help.business-loads.note4: Across a border the consignment note needs who receives the goods, their address and how many packages, and it asks for your instructions for customs. It says which law the carriage is under: the CMR where either country is a party to it, the Northern Corridor’s road protocol between its members, or else your contract.
help.business-loads.note5: Tick The carrier must have insurance cover and only a carrier whose insurance SeeBuyGet has checked off its policy, still running, can take the load — off the board, in offers and under a contract alike. Fewer carriers may answer. The consignment note says you asked for cover and names the carrier’s.
help.business-loads.note6: You may also declare a value for the goods and a special interest in delivery, and forbid transhipment. A declared value raises what the carrier answers for if the goods are lost or damaged, so a carrier may charge for it — agree it with them. Each goes on the consignment note; an order under a contract also shows the day it must arrive by.
help.business-loads.note7: If the driver notes something about the goods when taking them over — a torn sack, a loose wrap — it shows on the load, in “Papers”, under What the driver noted at pickup. It binds you only if you agree; dispute it and say why, and your words go on the consignment note beside the driver’s. You answer once.
help.business-loads.note3: The person who posted the load is also emailed a receipt when it is delivered, with a link to the consignment note.
help.business-loads.note8: Something wrong with what was delivered: open the load, then “Claim”, and “Report a problem with the goods” within seven days of delivery — damaged, short, or not received at all — in your own words, with a photo if you have one. SeeBuyGet judges no claim: unless a company of SeeBuyGet stated cover for the load, nobody of the network decides it or pays. Your words go onto the consignment note, and the note, frozen with them, is the damage claim report: hand it to the carrier or your insurer by a link, under Links to this note. Where the agreed trade term passed the risk to the receiver at the origin, the receiver claims, not you.
help.business-loads.note9: Refused at the door, whole or in part: the driver keeps the refused goods, and you say where they go within 48 hours — the load says by when. “Back to …” where they were picked up, “To another place”, or “Give them up”. Back or elsewhere, the driver who has them carries them as a new load at their vehicle’s price, and you pay it. Given up, nothing travels: the receiver may keep them, or the carrier disposes of them, and any cost of that is yours. With no answer in time they go back to where they were picked up, at your cost. Part refused: the rest was delivered and signed for as usual.
help.business-loads.note10: A load you pay the driver for directly: the driver says on the load when you have paid — or, once it is delivered, that you have not, and the load says “Not paid, says the driver”. If you did pay, “We paid — give the reference”: an M-Pesa code, a bank reference, or when and to whom you handed cash. One answer is kept; the driver is told, and drivers see it beside what the driver said, as disputed rather than unpaid. Still unpaid a week after the driver said so, with no answer from you, drivers are shown it before they take your loads. SeeBuyGet judges neither side.
help.business-loads.note11: Goods that fill a truck before they weigh it down — flowers, foam, empty crates — can say the space they take, under “Space it takes (m³), if it is light for its size”. A vehicle whose fleet recorded a smaller load space is not offered the load, and the board says by how much.
help.business-loads.note12: Moving an airline’s cargo by road under its air waybill and a flight number? Tick “Moved for an airline under its air waybill (a trucked flight)”, and give the waybill and the flight. It is carried as an ordinary road load under the law of the road: the waybill and the flight are a reference only, on the consignment note and told to the driver, and nobody on SeeBuyGet acts for the airline. Whether the air convention applies instead is not settled.
help.business-loads.note13: A load you have started is kept on this phone as you go, for three days, so a phone call does not lose it: Loads then offers “Carry on with the load you started” or “Start again”. It is gone from the phone once it is posted, and when you sign out.
help.business-loads.note14: Fresh or frozen food: on What it is, say the temperature it is kept at — chilled goods between 2 and 8 °C, frozen at -18 °C or colder, say between -25 and -18. Left empty, it is kept between 2 and 8 °C. Only a refrigerated or insulated truck is offered the load; the consignment note and its labels print the range, the driver logs the temperature on the way, and you are told under the bell if it leaves the range. The load’s Overview says the range it is kept in. A truck keeps one temperature, so it never carries your load beside another kept at a temperature the two cannot share.
help.business-coming-in.title: Receive goods at your own places
help.business-coming-in.summary: Business app, “Coming in”: what your suppliers send to your places, as it moves — your own order number, who it is from, how much, where it is now and who is bringing it. Never its price: that stays between you and your supplier.
help.business-coming-in.step1: “Coming in”, under Places. Under “Where you receive”, “Receive goods here” on one of your places gives it a code. Add the place under Business details first: a yard, a store, a factory gate.
help.business-coming-in.step2: “Send the code” passes it to a supplier, with how to use it. When they post a load, they tick “Deliver to another business, by the code it gave you” and type the code — with your order number, if you gave them one. The load comes to that place and shows here. The code names the place and nothing else of yours. “New code” makes the old one name nothing; “Stop receiving here” closes the place, and what was already sent there still shows.
help.business-coming-in.step3: Under “On its way to you”, each load: who it is from, how much, where it is, when it is expected and who is bringing it. “Follow it” opens its tracking page. From abroad, a line says whether it has cleared customs, and whose it is to clear by the agreed trade term: under DAP, clearing it in is yours.
help.business-coming-in.step4: Delivered, but not all as the note says — fewer packages, or some that are not the goods — what is missing stays under “Still expected” until you close it: “It came” when it arrives after all, or “Not coming” when you stop waiting, with a line for your records if you like. Your supplier is not told: what was found at the handover is already on its note.
help.business-coming-in.step5: Open a delivered load for “Your copy of the note”: the consignment note, kept for you as it was signed. The carriage price is on it only where the agreed trade term makes the carriage yours to pay. Pass it on by a link, as with your own loads.
help.business-coming-in.note1: A problem with what was delivered is yours to claim only where the agreed trade term passed the risk to you at the origin: then the load opened here has “Report a problem with the goods”, within seven days of delivery — damaged, short, or not received at all, with a photo if you have one. Otherwise your supplier claims, and the load says so. SeeBuyGet judges no claim: unless a company of SeeBuyGet stated cover for the load, nobody of the network decides it or pays, and your copy of the note, frozen with your claim on it, is the damage claim report for the carrier or your insurer.
help.business-coming-in.note2: A load you refuse at the door shows as “Refused at your door”. Where the goods go then is your supplier’s to say, and its to pay.
help.business-coming-in.note3: Why no price: what your supplier pays its carrier is between them, unless your trade term makes the carriage yours. The code shows a supplier the place, and nothing else of yours.
help.business-note.title: Download or pass on a consignment note
help.business-note.summary: Once the carrier has taken the goods over, the note is kept. Download it as one file, or make a link for somebody who has no account. When the load is delivered, a receipt is emailed with such a link in it.
